props.title: The Fountainhead

sections.content: The Fountainhead stands as Hollywood's most direct adaptation of Ayn Rand's objectivist philosophy, with Gary Cooper portraying Howard Roark, an uncompromising modernist architect who dynamites his own building rather than see his vision corrupted. The film's stark black-and-white cinematography by Robert Burks emphasizes the angular modernist architecture that becomes a character itself. Like Metropolis (1927) and The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari (1920) before it, The Fountainhead uses architecture as a visual metaphor for individualism versus collectivism, with Roark's clean lines contrasting against the traditional classical designs favored by the establishment.

sections.content: Architecture in film became a powerful storytelling device through the mid-20th century. Brazil (1985) used retro-futuristic design to criticize bureaucracy, while Blade Runner (1982) merged Art Deco with Asian influences to create its iconic dystopian cityscape. Mon Oncle (1958) satirized modernist architecture through Jacques Tati's playful lens, contrasting ultra-modern design with traditional French life. These films share The Fountainhead's preoccupation with how built environments shape human behavior and reflect societal values.

The film's treatment of creative integrity resonates with other Hollywood productions about artists fighting the system, like An American in Paris (1951) and 8½ (1963). However, The Fountainhead's extreme individualist stance - with Cooper's Roark willing to destroy his work rather than see it altered - represents a unique perspective in cinema. This theme of artistic purity versus commercial compromise would later echo in films like Barton Fink (1991) and Ed Wood (1994). SUBHEAD: Architectural Modernism in Post-War Cinema

sections.content: The Fountainhead arrived at a crucial moment when modernist architecture was transforming American cities. Its celebration of Howard Roark, partially inspired by Frank Lloyd Wright, reflected real tensions between innovative architects and conservative critics. Later films like The Pruitt-Igoe Myth (2011) and Visual Acoustics (2008) would document how modernist architectural ideals both succeeded and failed in practice. The film's stark visual style, emphasizing geometric shapes and dramatic angles, influenced later architectural documentaries like Koolhaas Houselife (2008) and My Architect (2003).
